title: News Article
description:
Saw the name in a portal news headline.

"Real estate broker Im arrested on suspicion of defrauding multiple investors"

There was a photo. Definitely Im Sangchul.

Separate from what {name} did — another case had surfaced elsewhere. The father's situation wasn't the only one.

Closed the article and looked out the window. Learned a lot from that man. That man destroyed his father. Both things are true at once.

choices.text: Just moved past it. That relationship is over.
choices.result_text:
Closed the article. The connection with Im Sangchul ended at that café.

Who {name} is now — got here without his help, and without his weight.

choices.text: Called his father. He should know about this.
choices.result_text:
"Yeah." Father said briefly. "Good."

Nothing more. A short silence. Something heavy lifted slightly.

choices.text: Feeling sorry for him is strange
choices.result_text:
Without that man, the {name} now might not exist. But that man destroyed his father.

Both are true simultaneously. That's uncomfortable.

title: Three Years Later
description:
Han Jiyeon's name appeared in a KakaoTalk alert. {name} would have had to scroll a long way to find where their last conversation ended. The new message was brief and polite.

"It's been a while. How have you been since then?"

Sangchul's introduction. The first short trades. A day when two different worlds had briefly touched. Two years had passed. "Life got busy" did not quite explain how neatly the silence had accumulated.

{name} opened the reply field. Before the typing indicator vanished, he had to decide how much truth to send.

choices.text: "I'm doing okay. Nice to hear from you." — straightforward
choices.result_text:
"I've been doing all right. It's good to hear from you."

Her reply came quickly. "I'm glad. I've been changing direction a little too. We should meet sometime." No date followed the invitation.

{name} sent a smiling face and closed the chat. They retreated again to the edges of each other's lives. This time, at least, one small light remained at the edge.

choices.text: "You helped me a lot back then. I think I've found my own way now." — honest
choices.result_text:
"You helped me a great deal back then. I think I've started finding my own way."

After a pause, Jiyeon asked, "What kind of way?" {name} expected to answer in a few lines. Writing about failed trades, salaries, and rebuilt rules gave the last two years a shape for the first time.

Jiyeon sent a long reply of her own. "I'm looking for something I can do under my own name too." After years of silence, the conversation resumed as though it had stopped yesterday.

title: An Empty Chair
description:
Forty-eight weeks had passed since Father died. The calendar marked the same place with one small dot.

There was no memorial table. In whatever room {name} now called home in Seoul, he stood Father's photograph beside the folded medicine packet. The room had changed; the work clothes and braced shoulders in the photograph had not.

He knew the distance to three billion won without opening a calculator. Today the harder figure was how he would explain that distance to Father.

"Did you have to suffer this much?" Father might have asked. Or perhaps, "What did you get for it?"

{name} placed an empty chair across from the photograph and sat for a long time.

choices.text: "I'll get there, Father." — said it inwardly
choices.result_text:
The words came out.

No one heard. Father isn't here. Did it anyway. That's what's possible right now.

choices.text: Wanted to explain the current situation to him
choices.result_text:
I'm at this point, Father. Still far. But not giving up.

{name} said all of it silently. Every word felt important.

choices.text: Turned on the monitor. Living people have things to do.
choices.result_text:
The monitor came on. The charts came up.

The photo was still there. {name} was still there. Living people have things to do.

title: The Cost of Knowing
description:
Two months since the last conversation with Im Sangchul.

Today, a real estate consultant {name} met through Sangchul's network sent a message.
An independent deal, no direct connection to Sangchul. Good return conditions.

{name} paused when first seeing the name.
Knew exactly where that contact chain started.

Use it knowing — or cut this whole network loose?

choices.text: Use it. This is my network now. His crimes don't transfer to me.
choices.result_text:
Closed the deal. Money came in.

Sangchul's name hovered faintly next to the consultant's — but that's only something {name} knows.

choices.text: Not doing this deal. If it came from there, it all gets cut.
choices.result_text:
Declined. Didn't say why.

Hanging up, {name} thought of the first day arriving in Seoul.
That {name} wouldn't have known what this deal was. Now knows. So cut it.

choices.text: Do the deal — but this is the last one. The line gets drawn here.
choices.result_text:
Said "last one" silently.

Whether that word was real — the only way to know was when the next similar call came.

title: Not Her Father's Company
description:
When they finally met, the corner of a thick exam guide protruded from Jiyeon's bag. She pushed it down while they waited for coffee, then spoke first.

"I'm studying for the licensed real-estate agent exam."

{name} stopped with his cup halfway raised. Her father ran a property company; she had once received early listings with a single phone call. He could not see why she would spend evenings adding highlighter marks to an exam book.

Jiyeon rested a hand on its cover as if she had expected the question. Her expression waited for a story about her, not her father's company.

choices.text: "Is it for your father's company?" — asked directly
choices.result_text:
"Is it for your father's company?"

Jiyeon gave the short smile of someone who had expected exactly that. "No. I want one thing that's mine. Something I can do under my own name, not as the property owner's daughter." Her fingertips pressed the book's cover.

{name} did not ask another question. For the first time, he understood that even someone born far ahead might need money and a place carrying only her own name. The word "mine" lingered longer than the coffee.

choices.text: "That exam isn't easy, is it?" — realistic
choices.result_text:
"That exam is difficult, isn't it?"

"It is." Jiyeon opened the guide to a page dense with notes. "That's why I want to do it. If it were easy, how would it be different from working for my father?"

{name} noticed how the page corners had worn soft. He did not fully understand why someone with every advantage would choose an inconvenient road. The frayed paper explained more accurately than she could.

choices.text: "I think you'll do great." — kept it light
choices.result_text:
"I think you'll do well. You've always been good at anything you try."

Jiyeon smiled and thanked him. The conversation moved on without harming the mood. The compliment was not false.

Only after they parted did {name} understand that he had praised what she already possessed without asking why she needed to build what she did not. Easy sentences always ended safely.

title: Different Directions
description:
A photograph of a train ticket arrived from Han Jiyeon, one way from Seoul Station to Busan.

"I'm moving down to Busan. I'm going to open a small brokerage under my own name."

{name} read the departure time and seat number three times for no reason. It was not sudden.

Jiyeon had studied and spoken of finding a direction outside her father's company. A plan he understood in theory acquired a different weight once it became a one-way ticket.

The cursor blinked in the reply field. On a screen, the distance between sending someone off and asking her to stay was only a few words.

choices.text: "Take care. Sincerely." — let her go
choices.result_text:
"Take care. I truly hope it works out."

Jiyeon replied, "Thank you. I'll call when I come up to Seoul." A blurred photograph of the platform arrived a moment later, taken through the train window.

{name} wrote nothing more and locked the screen. It felt as though he had sent her off properly, yet words remained in his hand. Even after the departure time passed, the final photograph in the chat did not move.

choices.text: "You should have done this ages ago." — honest
choices.result_text:
"You should have done this years ago."

After a pause, Jiyeon answered, "You're right. It's late." Another bubble followed. "Still, I'm glad it's now. Before it gets any later."

{name} studied the sentence. It did not seem meant only for the woman going to Busan. The one-way ticket quietly told him that it was not too late for him either.

choices.text: "You could stay here, you know." — wanted to hold her back
choices.result_text:
"You could stay here, you know."

The read receipt appeared, followed by a long silence. {name} began another sentence and stopped. At last, Jiyeon sent only, "Thank you." She did not say what she was thanking him for.

He had meant to hold her, but the conversation ended sooner instead. The departure time kept approaching unchanged. Only his words remained on the Seoul side.

title: Making the Call First
description:
Sunday morning.

No reason. Nothing to do.
{name} picked up the phone. Put it down. Picked it up again.

Thinking back — in almost three years, had almost never reached out first.
There was always a contact coming in. {name} was always the one receiving.

Today, decided to call first. No reason at all.

choices.text: Called his father. No reason.
choices.result_text:
Father picked up.
"Oh, Minjun?" His voice was warm with surprise.

Nothing special was said. Weather talk, "Have you eaten?" talk.
After hanging up, {name} realized:
That was the reason. You don't need one.

choices.text: Called Hyunsu. Haven't heard from him in a while.
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu picked up. "Hey? {name}? Been a while."

"Yeah. What are you up to?" — "Just studying." — "Same." — "...Want to eat?" — "When?" — "This week?"

That was that. One call made first became a plan a month out.

choices.text: Pressed the call button. Then hung up. Not yet.
choices.result_text:
Hung up before it could ring.

{name} wasn't sure why.
Turned the phone face-down on the desk and looked out the window.

Calling first turned out to be harder than expected.

title: A Call from Busan
description:
On a rainy night, Han Jiyeon called. It was the first time {name} had heard her voice since she moved to Busan, almost a year ago.

"The deal closed. A small villa in Goejeong-dong. My first sale from start to finish."

She did not sound as lightly triumphant as she once had. Papers shifted and a bus braked outside her office at the other end of the call.

Jiyeon laughed, caught her breath, then spoke longer about the instant her own stamp met the contract than about the price.

Before congratulating her, {name} wondered why she had wanted him to hear this first.

choices.text: "That's great. Genuinely. You made it happen."
choices.result_text:
"That's wonderful. You carried it from beginning to end."

The line went quiet for a moment. Jiyeon laughed softly. "It finally feels real when you say it, oppa. I didn't call just anyone tonight."

{name} watched rain travel down the window instead of answering. A first contract in Busan and a night in Seoul occupied the same call. For a moment, the year's distance narrowed to the width of a voice.

choices.text: "Can I say I've missed you? After this long?"
choices.result_text:
"May I finally say that I've missed you?"

The papers went still. Jiyeon drew a short breath before laughing. "I wanted to hear that. I missed you too." Her usually poised voice dropped on the final words.

After the call, {name} stared at the ceiling. The bus outside her Busan office was gone, but the half beat in which she had inhaled remained in his ear.

choices.text: "I'm holding on here too. Each in our own direction."
choices.result_text:
"I'm holding on here too. Each in our own direction."

Jiyeon was quiet, then said, "Yes. We're both still on the way." The celebratory call soon ended with ordinary questions about life.

Different directions was still a true phrase. After they hung up, the Seoul night and the lights of her Busan office seemed level for one moment, then moved apart again.

title: Briefly in Seoul
description:
Jiyeon came up to Seoul for two days of continuing education. A KTX ticket back to Busan the next morning was folded into the side pocket of her bag.

They met not in some glittering Cheongdam café, but in a small place near {name}'s neighborhood.

Jiyeon watched the street for a long time. "Seoul feels strangely unfamiliar. It's only been a year." She took two sips without setting down the cup.

"Still, having you here makes it feel like Seoul again, oppa."

She kept the line light, but one finger slowly traced the paper cup's seam. Tomorrow, she would be back in Busan.

choices.text: "Come often then. I'll be waiting."
choices.result_text:
"Then come often. I'll be waiting."

Jiyeon looked up. She began with her usual poised smile, then let it soften half a beat later. "May I come whenever I want?" "Whenever."

They walked together to the subway after leaving the café. The silence was not awkward. At the gate, Jiyeon adjusted the bag holding her Busan ticket. The promise to wait settled quietly on the shoulders of someone who still had to return.

choices.text: "Don't let this dismantle what you built in Busan. That's real, what you made there."
choices.result_text:
"Don't dismantle the life you built in Busan. What you made there is real."

Jiyeon touched the rim of her cup for a long time. "Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. I wasn't asking you to hold me back."

Her ticket south remained unchanged. When they parted, her step looked lighter than when she arrived. {name} learned that he could face someone without pulling her toward him.

choices.text: (Couldn't find words. That was the answer.)
choices.result_text:
{name} looked only at his cup. He could say neither that he would wait nor that returning to Busan was all right. As the silence lengthened, Jiyeon picked up her bag.

"I should go. I have class again tomorrow." Her politeness remained perfectly composed.

Two cold coffees stayed on the table after the door closed. The answer he never gave left the space between them before her train did.

title: Back to Seoul
description:
A photograph arrived from Jiyeon in Busan: the key to a new office, tagged with an address in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. Her message followed.

"I've decided to open a Seoul branch next month. The Busan office will keep operating."

One more line appeared. "I wanted to tell you first, oppa."

{name} reread the part that said she was not closing Busan to return. Jiyeon had built a name there and was carrying that name into a wider city.

Though the key could not touch his hand, its metal looked cold. Their directions might meet again in the same place.

choices.text: "See you in Gangnam. I'm on my way there too."
choices.result_text:
"See you in Gangnam. I'm on my way there too."

After the read receipt, Jiyeon's answer arrived. "Then I'll see you in Gangnam, oppa. For sure." The formality disappeared for the first time. The sentence was short, and therefore unmistakable.

{name} saved the office address on his map. Neither had fully arrived, but this time they were moving toward the same promise. The familiar map of Seoul looked, for a moment, like another city.

choices.text: "That decision has to be yours. Not because of me."
choices.result_text:
"The decision has to be for you. It cannot be because of me."

Jiyeon answered after a pause. "I know. It is for me. I'm more certain because I built something in Busan first. But you are one of the reasons, oppa."

{name} did not try to correct the sentence. Her year in Busan had proved the difference between including someone in a reason and abandoning herself for him. The key in the photograph still rested beneath her own name.

title: Word from Busan
description:
Jiyeon's name came up over lunch with a mutual contact. Her Busan office had settled in; she had hired staff and earned a local reputation for careful work. News {name} had not asked for arrived one piece at a time across the table.

The contact took a drink of water, then added, "Oh, and I hear she's seeing someone there. Someone from Busan."

{name}'s chopsticks stopped above a side dish. Relief that she was doing well arrived beside the knowledge that seasons he knew nothing about had accumulated.

Neither feeling was false, which made it difficult to give the whole thing one name.

choices.text: "That's great." — said it sincerely
choices.result_text:
"That's wonderful. I mean it."

Once the words were out, {name} knew they were true. In Busan, Jiyeon had built an office and relationships under her own name. The "something of mine" she once described had become a life concrete enough for other people to report.

The conversation moved on. {name} picked up the cold side dish. "Different directions" had first sounded like goodbye. Today it remained as the sentence that had let neither of them be wrong.

choices.text: (Nodded. Nothing to say.)
choices.result_text:
{name} only nodded. Congratulations reached his throat and stopped. It was not that he had nothing to say; something remained that was no longer his to say.

After lunch, he stepped into the street alone. The signal changed and people crossed as always. Nothing in Seoul looked different.

Somewhere unseen, a new season that had begun in Busan continued without him.

description_if_known.jiyeon_respectfully_distanced:
Jiyeon's name came up over lunch. Her Busan office had settled in; she had hired staff and made a name locally. Then came the news that she was seeing someone there.

{name}'s chopsticks paused, but he soon said, "That's wonderful." When Jiyeon visited Seoul, he had honestly told her there was someone in his life. She had neither clung to him nor blamed him. Afterward, she had spoken of Busan with greater ease.

A door closed properly did not invite anyone to look through its cracks. That was why today's news could arrive shaped more like congratulations than regret.
description_if_known.jiyeon_hidden_feelings:
Jiyeon's name came up over lunch. Her Busan office had settled in; she had hired staff and made a name locally. Then came the news that she was seeing someone there.

{name}'s chopsticks stopped. When Jiyeon visited Seoul, he had chosen silence, and she had left two cold coffees behind. A conversation left unfinished hardens into different sentences inside each person.

That day's silence remained between congratulations and regret. There was no one left to ask what meaning time had given it.

title: Briefly in Seoul (Two Hearts)
description:
Jiyeon came to Seoul. Two-day continuing education for licensed brokers.

The same café. Jiyeon spoke first. "Seoul feels strangely unfamiliar. It's only been a year."

After two sips of coffee, she added: "Having you here makes it feel like Seoul again, oppa."

{name} paused.
Knew the weight of those words. And also — knew there was already someone else.

choices.text: Said it honestly. "I'm seeing someone right now."
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon was quiet for a moment. Then smiled. "I know. I just mean — you're a good person."

They finished their coffee. It wasn't awkward.

Learned that day — honest words don't break things.

choices.text: (Said nothing. Let her misread it.)
choices.result_text:
Said nothing.

Jiyeon smiled and stood up. "See you again."

{name} sat there. The gap between 'not being honest' and 'lying' — narrower than expected.

title: Twelve Minutes Before Departure
description:
Twelve minutes before the Busan train departed, {name} stepped onto the platform at Seoul Station. Jiyeon stood beneath the seat number on the departure board, one hand around the handle of a small suitcase. The one-way ticket he had seen in a photograph trembled inside a clear sleeve, now a real piece of paper.

"I didn't think you would actually come, Minjun."

Jiyeon smiled, but did not let go of the suitcase. Her plan to open a brokerage in Busan under her own name was already set. So was the look saying she would not wait for anyone to ask her to remain in Seoul. The boarding announcement urged them on. Between them stood one bag and one sentence still unspoken. Words might hold her feet for a moment; they could not change the direction printed on the ticket.

choices.text: "I want to ask you not to go. I'm not ready to let you leave."
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon's hand stopped on the suitcase handle. She listened to the end, then spoke quietly. "I did want to hear that. But I still have to go. If I stay, I think I may blame you for it someday."

When the doors opened, Jiyeon took the first step back. {name} had finally brought his hidden feeling into the open, but he could not use it to make her surrender something bearing her own name. Their eyes held until the doors closed between them.

choices.text: "Take care. Congratulations on beginning something under your own name."
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon smiled half a beat late. "Thank you. I think I'll remember that for a long time."

{name} carried the suitcase across the boarding line and released it at once. He attached neither a plea nor a future promise. Jiyeon bowed once from inside the train. He had sent her off properly. In exchange, one sentence that belonged to this moment alone stayed behind on the platform.

choices.text: "I won't answer now. I'll tell you when you come back."
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon looked at the board, then at {name}. "Then there is no answer today." Her voice remained courteous, leaving no opening to revise what he had said.

The conductor gestured beside the door. Jiyeon pulled her suitcase aboard. She did not promise to return, and {name} did not promise to wait. Once the train began to move, only the postponed answer remained in his mouth as a complete sentence.

title: The Empty Platform
description:
At 9:12 p.m., {name} stood alone at the far end of a transfer platform in Seoul Station. Eleven minutes remained until the next train. He had come to see no one off, and no one was waiting for him. Then Father called from Changwon.

"Minjun. About that debt. There was a man named Park Sang-jin. A real-estate man named Lim in Gangnam introduced him and said he could be trusted."

Father paused behind the unfinished name. A platform announcement reported the approaching train; a television murmured through the phone from Changwon. On a night with no departing lover to claim this stretch of time, a family sentence ten years late arrived instead. The question was no longer whom to call, but how much to hear from the person already connected.

choices.text: "Do you remember any more of that man's name?" — let the train go and ask
choices.result_text:
Over the sound of opening doors, Father answered. "It was Lim. I'm sure of the family name, but I can't remember the rest now."

{name} did not move from the boarding line. The doors closed, leaving only the train's wind. The next connection was forty minutes away, and the blank in the name remained. What he could write down exactly was the limit of Father's memory: the surname Lim.

choices.text: "Why are you telling me only now?" — hear the rest
choices.result_text:
After a long pause, Father said, "You had already paid it all. Telling you felt like putting one more thing on your back. But I thought you should know."

The train arrived and departed while neither man ended the call. {name} did not learn the introducer's full name, but for the first time he heard why Father had kept silent. The train's red tail lights and a late apology receded together beyond the platform.

choices.text: Board without interrupting and hear Father to the end
choices.result_text:
{name} crossed the doors just before they closed, but did not end the call. After a long breath Father said, "I just thought I had to tell you now. I'm sorry, son."

{name} kept the phone to his ear until there were no more words. He made the connection and heard the confession to its end. The chance to ask the introducer's full name, or why Father had waited, passed in the noise of the train. The call log kept three minutes and seventeen seconds.

title: The Witness Queue Number
description:
The sheet fresh from the police case window was still warm beneath the fluorescent lights. The witness attendance notice carried the report filing number at the top and today's queue number, 47, below the perforation. On one page, finishing the report and surrendering more of his own time had been fastened together.

Behind the clear partition, the clerk told {name} not to fold it twice. "When your number is called, use the interview room on the right." Toner and wet umbrellas mixed in the corridor lined with gray plastic chairs. {name} covered the case number with one finger and spread the queue number across his knees. The display advanced one place at a time, counting an afternoon the original filing had not taken.

choices.text: Open the notice across his knees and sit in the witness waiting area
choices.result_text:
{name} sat in the gray waiting row and held his thumb over the perforation dividing the filing number from the queue number. A drop from the umbrella beside him ran across the floor tile.

Each chime from the display made the lower edge of the sheet tremble. The filing receipt proved an act already finished; the attached 47 counted the time being given today. {name} kept the paper unfolded and listened for the next call.

title: The Distance in Cold Coffee
description:
For their first meeting after the forgiveness, Sangchul sat by the window of a small café two alleys from the old real-estate office. The foam had fallen from both coffees, and a thin brown skin had formed around {name}'s cup. Sangchul started to push a sugar packet toward the center, then drew back his hand.

"Since you came, perhaps we can at least have coffee like before."

{name} left two handspans of bare table between them. "I accepted the apology. I did not accept the words like before."

Sangchul rotated his cup without smiling. Cold coffee left a ring on the saucer. The forgiveness had already been given; what it did not erase now occupied a measurable distance between their chairs.

choices.text: Take one sip of the cold coffee and set the cup between them
choices.result_text:
{name} swallowed the cold coffee. Bitterness arrived before the aroma. He pulled the cup toward neither man and set it at the table's center, where its wet ring crossed the empty space.

Sangchul seemed to swallow the words he had prepared and folded only the corner of the sugar packet. Both men watched the same ring without mentioning the instant coffee from the old office. {name} left half the cup untouched and pressed his back to the chair.

title: The Priority Badge with an Introducer
description:
The printer at the financial counseling desk pushed out a badge and a fee sheet in succession. Beneath {name}'s name, the white badge said PRIORITY in heavy type and, in smaller letters, "Introducer: Lim Sangchul." Beside it, the standard fee sheet listed the ordinary cost and waiting order for the same consultation.

The clerk fitted the badge into a clear clip. "They will check this in the front line. Keep the fee sheet with you." People in the general queue held the same sheet folded around their numbered tickets. The faster place and lower fee {name} had already gained had become a mark worn on his chest. Sangchul's name was smaller than the benefit, but it remained directly under his own.

choices.text: Clip on the priority badge and enter the front line with the fee sheet open
choices.result_text:
{name} clipped the badge to his shirt. Its plastic corner scratched his chest once; the standard amount stayed visible beneath his palm on the open sheet.

When the clerk pointed to the priority line, several numbered tickets shifted behind him. {name} stepped inside the front marker without folding the prices out of sight. His pager sounded first, and the small words "Introducer: Lim Sangchul" moved forward with his body.

title: The Dates on Two Sheets
description:
The transaction history came from the bank kiosk carrying the heat of fresh toner. One line read "Sender: Lim Sangchul" beside the returned amount. {name} took Father's old paid-in-full certificate from the inner pocket of his wallet. The red stamp had cracked along every fold, and repeated handling had rounded the corners.

Under the kiosk's white lamp, the amounts overlapped when he held the pages together; the dates remained far apart. The statement printed today showed exactly when the money had arrived. The old certificate held the time his son had already finished paying. A prompt sounded for the next customer. In {name}'s hands were two matching numbers and two dates that no column could combine.

choices.text: Align the transaction record and certificate beneath the kiosk light
choices.result_text:
{name} matched the final digits on both sheets. The numbers occupied one line, but the cracks in the paid stamp would not match the smooth new statement.

Someone sorting coins behind him coughed, and {name} cleared the kiosk. He placed the fresh page at the front of a clear folder and Father's certificate behind it. Even after the folder closed, the white distance between the two dates showed through.

title: A New Seat Outside the List
description:
At the entrance to a small redevelopment briefing, registered guests collected QR badges. {name}'s name was absent from the reception tablet. While the clerk searched again, an usher emerged from a side door and handed him a seat slip marked B-17 in pen and a white introduction card. It had no issue number or stamp, only the words "Introduced by Lim Sangchul."

"Your name stays off the list. We only held the seat." The usher pointed to the closed side door, not the registration desk. The silence in which {name} had agreed to ask no more about the truth had been used first as permission for an unrecorded favor. Chairs scraped inside. Among guests wearing printed badges, B-17 waited with only a paper seat slip.

choices.text: Place the introduction card under the program and sit in B-17
choices.result_text:
{name} passed the registration tablet and walked to the marked row. Unlike the other chairs, B-17 had no printed badge on its back. He slid the introduction card under the program, leaving only the last letters of Sangchul's name visible.

The folding chair gave a short cry when {name} sat. The official list remained blank while one real body entered the room. The usher removed the handwritten seat slip, put it in a pocket, and returned through the side door.

title: The Unmarked Envelope at the Management Office
description:
A yellow document envelope waited on the storage rack in the management office of {name}'s current building. Only his name and unit appeared on the front; there was no sender, postal stamp, or tracking number. The manager opened the handover ledger. "Someone from Lim Sangchul's Sinchon office left it in person. They only asked us to confirm the resident."

The current address {name} had kept outside their contact after cutting ties was written carefully across the envelope. The corner of a rectangular document pressed through the thin paper, but no title showed. The elevator home stood beside the management-office door. The relationship he had ended was waiting neither by phone nor at Sangchul's office, but in the storage slot beside the entrance he crossed every day.

choices.text: Sign the management ledger and take the envelope with its seal intact
choices.result_text:
{name} checked the unit and his name, then signed the receipt column. When the manager passed him the envelope, the paper inside slid once; the glued flap remained closed.

The elevator mirror reflected his current address on the front. The management ledger now held the received time, but its sender field was blank. As the doors closed, {name} did not break the seal. He held only the edges with both hands.

title: The Choice Father Heard
description:
When Father answered, {name} did not begin by asking how he was. He named Park Sang-jin, repeated that Sangchul had introduced and vouched for him, described Sangchul's reaction in the café, and said exactly what answer he had given there. He neither softened nor shortened the words he had spoken in the café.

The television went silent in Changwon. Father did not interrupt. Even after the last sentence, he said nothing for a long time. Then he asked quietly, "So are you all right now?"

It was not a question about whether {name} had done right or wrong. On his desk lay whatever paper the choice had left. On the line waited the man whose guarantee had begun the debt. Only the focus of the explanation remained to be chosen.

choices.text: Explain the records and his actions in chronological order
choices.result_text:
{name} recited everything, from the case number on the paid-in-full certificate to the record now in his hands. Father listened to the end. "Trusting that man was my part," he said. "Don't turn your choice into another piece of my debt."

The facts lay precisely between them. {name} never managed to say he had been afraid. The call became orderly, but his son's voice remained as dry as a report.

choices.text: "What I did after that was my choice. I won't make excuses."
choices.result_text:
Father drew a short breath. "Right. If you chose it, you have to look at it." After a pause he added, "That doesn't mean you have to look alone."

{name} did not use Sangchul or the debt as an excuse. In taking responsibility back into his own sentence, he also gave up the chance to say why he had chosen that way. They remained connected in silence for a while.

choices.text: "When you wrote your name in the guarantor field, what did Sangchul say?"
choices.result_text:
Father was silent a long time. "He said Park Sang-jin could be trusted. Said I only had to fill in the guarantor field." His voice fell. "I suppose I wanted to believe him too."

{name} pictured the paper at the other end of the line. He finally recovered the sentence spoken over the guarantee, but the words meant to explain his own choice stopped before it. After the call ended, ‘only the guarantor field’ remained in the room.

title: The Copies Hyunsu Opened
description:
At a corner table in the café, Hyunsu aligned the copies {name} had handed him from the first page: the case number on the paid-in-full certificate, Park Sang-jin in the article, and Lim Sangchul in the closed registry. {name} had already told him what Sangchul said in the café and what answer he gave. The facts now lay before Hyunsu and could not be redirected to someone else.

Hyunsu stared at the papers before speaking. "Hyung, so that man knew who you were from the beginning?" When {name} nodded, Hyunsu's fingertips stopped. "This isn't something that ends because the numbers match."

It was neither comfort nor a verdict. Copies and cooling coffee remained between them. He now had to decide how much of the burden to place in Hyunsu's hands.

choices.text: Add nothing and let him review every number and original line
choices.result_text:
While matching dates, Hyunsu underlined the redacted final-digit field in the article. "This part has to stay unknown, hyung. You can't write it as if it matches."

{name} erased one overconfident line from his notes. The record became more honest. For a while, however, they sat not as friends but as reviewer and submitter. Hyunsu's first question received no emotional answer.

choices.text: Before the documents, tell his friend why he brought the story here
choices.result_text:
{name} said he was not asking Hyunsu to judge. He simply did not want to be the only person who knew. Hyunsu folded the copies and set them down. "Then I won't ask whether you did the right thing. I'll ask whether you're all right now."

The numerical review remained unfinished. Hyunsu looked at {name} instead of the paper. Time for arranging facts and time for remaining friends exchanged places.

choices.text: "Just hear me. Don't contact Sangchul or investigate further."
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu bit his lip, then slid the copies back toward {name}. "All right. I won't move without your permission. But don't make it into something that never happened, hyung."

The boundary became exact. So did the loss of any investigation or call Hyunsu might have shared. {name} gathered the copies again while Hyunsu, empty-handed, held only his coffee cup.

title: The Unsent Sentence
description:
Late that night, after the month's appointments and alerts had all gone quiet, {name} sat alone at the desk in his current room. An unsent sentence remained open on the laptop: ‘I need to tell you about Sangchul.’ The recipient field was blank. The fact that no one had heard him this month was visible as one empty box.

Beside it lay a personal clear folder holding the paid-in-full certificate and a folded copy of the article. It was not a copy being filed anywhere, nor an envelope promised to anyone. Each past hour already carried its mark on the calendar; none could be taken back and spent on a different act. Only the aftermath of being unheard remained: save the dated statement, seal the personal copy without a destination, or erase the draft and keep one question for later.

choices.text: Keep the unsent statement in his notebook with the date
choices.result_text:
{name} copied down the answer he had given Sangchul and what frightened him now. At the bottom he added the date and, ‘Heard by no one.’

The sequence of the case and his own words remained. A recipient never appeared. When he closed the notebook, the loss became clearer: recording something exactly and telling it to another person were not the same act.

choices.text: Seal the personal copies in an envelope with no destination
choices.result_text:
{name} ordered the paid-in-full certificate and article copy, then placed them in an envelope. On the front he wrote only today's date and ‘personal copies.’ He added no recipient.

The pages could no longer scatter, but the choice inside them reached no human voice. Once the envelope closed, the unsent sentence remained open on the screen and the room's silence grew more solid.

choices.text: Delete the draft and leave only ‘Who can I say this in front of?’ on the calendar
choices.result_text:
{name} erased the long statement and emptied the trash. In the next blank space on the calendar he wrote only, ‘Who can I say this in front of?’ He attached neither a person's name nor a time.

The question remained; today's exact words disappeared. No one having heard him remained true as well. In the dark screen, his face overlapped faintly with a question that had no one waiting for it.

title: The Last Call Beside the Medicine Bag
description:
The phone lit beside the folded medicine bag. The call history held the date and duration of Father's last connected call. There was no recording; the only voice {name} could hear again was his memory of Father's first word: “Minjun.”

Beside it lay the copy bearing Daeun's handwritten scope and deadline from the four-person meeting, with Father's old guarantee comparison beneath. One page defined how far its owner's name could be used; the other held a name already set inside someone else's request.

The calendar stayed closed. The call history held only a date and duration; the folded medicine bag carried no diagnosis or sentence that could settle what followed. In this room, he could only choose one sentence to leave in his own voice before the connected-call record and two documents.

choices.text: Say, “This time I read the liability before the guarantor field”
choices.result_text:
“This time I did not write a name first. I read where the liability ended.”

{name}'s voice fell between the medicine bag and the phone. No praise and no rebuke returned.

He placed the comparison with Jaehyuk's PDF beside Father's document instead of over it. Between the two guarantor fields remained a space wide enough for one finger.

choices.text: Place Daeun's handwritten limit beside Father's signature and admit what was never asked
choices.result_text:
{name} aligned Daeun's sentence—I DO NOT CONSENT BEYOND THESE TERMS—with Father's settled signature.

“Back then, I looked at how urgent the request was before asking whose name was being borrowed. I should have asked first.”

The sentence could not persuade a photograph. Daeun's hand and Father's signature remained on the same desk without touching. The folded corner of the medicine bag rose between them.

choices.text: Close the documents and read aloud only the date and duration of the last call
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the comparison and handwritten copy in turn. He read the date and call duration from the screen once each.

“I answered that call.”

He added no explanation. This time, the chance to say how he had handled another person's name folded away as well. On the darkened screen, only the white medicine bag and {name}'s lips showed faintly.

title: A Call Between Two Names
description:
At 11:18 p.m., the call {name} placed connected on the third ring. A television quieted in Changwon. Father said, “Minjun, what brings you this late?”

On the desk lay Jiyeon's limited-consent copy, carrying the boundary she wrote herself and Minseo's review mark, beside Father's old guarantee. One name had a written end to its liability. The older signature had hardened inside years when no one asked where liability ended.

“I'm looking at your document beside the consent I received today.”

Father was quiet, then said, “All right. You called first, so say it one thing at a time.” {name} swallowed the greeting he had prepared. One question remained to be finished between the two pages.

choices.text: Read Jiyeon's liability boundary and ask whether Father saw his own
choices.result_text:
{name} read Jiyeon's line first: I DO NOT CONSENT BEYOND THIS SCOPE. “When you signed, did you see where your liability ended?”

Something rasped on Father's end, like paper turning. “Back then I didn't look for the ending. I heard that someone was desperate first.”

{name} did not copy that sentence into the margin of Jiyeon's consent. Today's boundary had become clear; whom Father had seen first remained only inside the call.

choices.text: Read the names on the old guarantee and ask why Father did not ask first
choices.result_text:
{name} read the debtor's name above Father's signature, then the guarantor field. “Did you ask why their debt had to become yours?”

Father breathed out once. “I didn't. Did you ask her first today?”

The question returned unchanged. {name} pressed a finger to Jiyeon's handwritten boundary. He had received one answer from Father and lost his remaining room to evade his own.

choices.text: Admit he nearly began with Jiyeon's name and ask Father only to listen
choices.result_text:
“I calculated with Jiyeon's name before asking her. This time she wrote the limit herself.”

{name} kept the two sentences in that order and added no defense. Father said, “All right. I'm listening now. Don't add more than what you actually did.”

Only the sound of a page turning continued through the receiver. On the desk, Jiyeon's boundary and Father's old signature heard the same voice without touching.

title: Zero Seconds, No Answer
description:
Father's name remained in Contacts after his death. When {name} opened the details of the last outgoing attempt, the date sat above NO ANSWER — 0:00. There was no voice to hear and no recording that explained why the call had not connected.

Beside the phone lay the folded medicine bag, printed only with dosing times, and a copy of Father's old guarantee. Beneath them rested {name}'s self-name draft after Daeun had written her refusal and removed her own name. One object held a contact that never connected; the other held a document not yet filed even after another name was removed.

The date, zero seconds, and medicine bag said no more than that. He could only decide how to leave those three verified things together now.

choices.text: Copy the last outgoing date and 0:00 onto the back of his self-name draft
choices.result_text:
{name} copied the date and 0:00 from the screen onto the back of the draft without changing a character. Beneath them he wrote only NO ANSWER.

Why Father could not answer, and what he might have said, remained blank. The page waiting for his own name had gained one heavier line, but that line did not become a final conversation.

choices.text: Record only the fact that the call never connected in his own voice
choices.result_text:
{name} opened a new voice memo. “The last call I placed never connected. Its duration was zero seconds. Today I'm looking at a document that removes another person's name and leaves mine.”

He stopped there. The file held no voice from Father, only his breathing and the refrigerator in the room. The record grew exact; the person it could not reach grew clearer.

choices.text: Photograph only the medicine bag and call screen, adding no explanation
choices.result_text:
{name} captured the call log, photographed the folded medicine bag's dosing times, and placed the two images side by side. The last outgoing date, 0:00, and dosing times fit in one image; he gave it only the date as its title.

The old guarantee and self-name draft stayed on the desk outside the frame. The white medicine bag and black zero filled the image; today's name fields remained beyond the lens.

title: News Article
description:
Saw the name in a portal news headline.

"Real estate broker Im arrested on suspicion of defrauding multiple investors"

There was a photo. Definitely Im Sangchul.

Separate from what {name} did — another case had surfaced elsewhere. The father's situation wasn't the only one.

Closed the article and looked out the window. Learned a lot from that man. That man destroyed his father. Both things are true at once.

choices.text: Just moved past it. That relationship is over.
choices.result_text:
Closed the article. The connection with Im Sangchul ended at that café.

Who {name} is now — got here without his help, and without his weight.

choices.text: Opened Father's number — wanting to tell him the news.
choices.result_text:
Father's name and number remained in Contacts. {name} tapped Share on the article, then stopped at the recipient field.

He wanted to tell him that more victims had surfaced, that what happened to Father had not been the only case. But this was no longer a number that could connect. The link was never sent.

When he closed the article, nothing heavy had lifted. Only the absence of anyone who could hear this news had become clearer.

choices.text: Feeling sorry for him is strange
choices.result_text:
Without that man, the {name} now might not exist. But that man destroyed his father.

Both are true simultaneously. That's uncomfortable.
